solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Suggesting my words are false introduces pressure (8)

indicatorNotes.introduces: to introduce something is to bring it in, so the phrase brings P in among its letters

blocks.note: what the speaker would say: I'M LYING
P = pressure, set between I'M and LYING

annotation.surface: Someone owning up that what they say is a sham, under pressure.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue is a paraphrase to be turned back into speech: 'my words are false' is a confession you would say aloud in the first person.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: implying means suggesting something without stating it outright.

entries.clue: Entertainer accepting a dodgy role on stage (7)

indicatorNotes.accepting: to accept something is to take it in, so MC takes A into itself

annotation.surface: A performer taking on a shady character in a play.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Duff' is British slang for faulty or useless, which is what 'dodgy' means here.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Macduff, the thane who kills Macbeth, is one part in Shakespeare's play.

entries.clue: Athlete ably running in set places (3,3,5)

indicatorNotes.running: letters that are running about are loose and moving, so they settle in a new order

annotation.surface: A runner competing well in set positions on a track.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Running' looks like the athlete's event, and 'set places' like starting blocks; both belong to the dining room instead.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: setting places, the cutlery and plates for each diner, is what laying the table means.

entries.clue: Youngster losing head hands round drug, one unlikely to work (5)

indicatorNotes.losing head: a word's head is its first letter, so losing it drops the K
indicatorNotes.round: to go round something is to surround it, so L and R sit either side of E

blocks.note: E = ecstasy, held between L and R

annotation.surface: A decapitated youngster passing drugs around: a dark crime picture.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hands' is not a verb here: it is the pair of hands, left and right, which wrap round the drug.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive paraphrase: an idler is lazy, and so someone unlikely to do any work.

entries.clue: Socialist Party in summer time uprising (7)

indicatorNotes.in: one thing in another is inside it, so RAVE sits inside AUG
indicatorNotes.uprising: rising up, which in a down clue means the letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: a rave is a party, placed inside AUG: ARAVEUG

annotation.surface: A left-wing party staging a revolt in the summer.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface's politics are real: Che Guevara led revolutions, so 'uprising' fits both the scene and the direction of reading.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Che Guevara, the Argentine Marxist revolutionary, is one famous socialist.

entries.clue: Revolutionary has fun pets (6)

indicatorNotes.Revolutionary: a revolution is a turn right round, so the word is turned to read backwards

annotation.surface: A rebel enjoying the company of animals.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pets' are not animals but sulks, as in 'in a pet'; a strop is British slang for a bad-tempered sulk.
annotation.definitionFit: A less common sense: a pet is a fit of sulking, which in British slang is a strop.

entries.clue: Game is fine, with Reds put in new positions on the wings (4,5)

indicatorNotes.put in new positions: letters placed in new positions are rearranged
indicatorNotes.on the wings: wings are the two sides, so the rearranged letters flank OK

blocks.note: fine = OK, sitting in the middle

annotation.surface: A football report: a manager happy to move his Reds players out to the wings.
annotation.walkthrough: The football picture hides that 'put' is fodder, not an instruction: the letters of REDS PUT are what move.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: stud poker, where some cards are dealt face up, is one card game.

entries.clue: Half-hearted, cross staff (3)

indicatorNotes.Half-hearted: with only half a heart, so the double-O middle keeps just one O

blocks.note: a rood is a cross, especially in a church

annotation.surface: Grumpy staff who can't be bothered.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like an adjective next to 'Half-hearted'; it is the noun, the old word rood.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a staff is a long stick, which is a rod.

entries.clue: Sign nothing’s missing in substandard holiday accommodation (7)

indicatorNotes.missing: something missing is absent, so the O is taken out of the phrase

annotation.surface: A complaint that there's nothing laid on in a shabby campsite.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sign' reads as a noticeboard at the campsite; it is an omen.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a portent is a sign or omen of something to come.

entries.clue: Ruler favouring the Tories crows, stifling unknown protest forcefully (3,4,6)

indicatorNotes.stifling: to stifle is to smother, so the chain closes over the unknown

blocks.note: a murder of crows is the collective noun

annotation.surface: A Conservative-leaning monarch gloating while silencing an anonymous critic.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crows' reads as a verb, gloats; it is the birds. Tories are the British Conservatives, whose party colour is blue.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to cry blue murder is to make a loud, outraged fuss, a forceful protest.

entries.clue: Retailer’s opening guide for one making a career (6)

indicatorNotes.opening: a word's opening is where it starts, its first letter

blocks.note: an usher guides people to seats

annotation.surface: A shop's starter manual for someone building a working life.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Career' here is the verb, to rush headlong, not a profession.
annotation.definitionFit: A less common sense: to career is to hurtle along, so one making a career is a rusher.

entries.clue: They may hold drugs from ace smugglers smuggling a lot of marijuana (8)

indicatorNotes.smuggling: smugglers hide goods inside, so MULES carry PO hidden within
indicatorNotes.a lot of: a lot of something is most but not all of it, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: POT without its T, tucked in MULES

annotation.surface: A narcotics story: an expert gang of couriers hiding a stash of cannabis.
annotation.walkthrough: The drug-running scene is consistent throughout, but the drugs in the definition are medicines in sealed glass phials.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: ampoules are small sealed glass vials that hold injectable medicine.

entries.clue: Account not meriting credit or PIN in refined neighbourhood’s banks (5,6)

indicatorNotes.in: one thing in another is inside it, so LEG goes inside URBANE
indicatorNotes.banks: a river's banks are its two edges, so only the first and last letters count

blocks.note: pins = legs, informally; LEG goes before URBANE's last E
first and last letters of neighbourhood

annotation.surface: Banking jargon: an account refused credit, or a PIN problem at the posh local bank.
annotation.walkthrough: The capitals of PIN point to a card number, but it is a leg, as in 'shaky on his pins'. 'Credit' means belief, not a loan.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: an urban legend is a story widely told but not worth believing.

entries.clue: Wide, rotten boat full of animals covers miles (3,3,4)

indicatorNotes.covers: to cover something is to go over and round it, so THE ARK encloses M

annotation.surface: A leaky, overloaded vessel spread over miles of water.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wide' looks like a size for the boat; it is the adjective for a missed shot or a bowl that strays from its target.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a shot that goes wide misses its target, so it is off the mark.

entries.clue: Pernod drunk hot and cool? It makes you feel good (9)

indicatorNotes.drunk: a drunk staggers about, so the letters lurch into a new order

annotation.surface: A drinker praising an aniseed spirit taken hot or chilled.
annotation.walkthrough: The drinking surface makes 'It makes you feel good' sound like the Pernod; it is the body's own chemical. Pernod is a French aniseed liqueur.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: endorphins are hormones the body releases that produce a sense of wellbeing.

entries.clue: It holds large quantity of alcohol still ultimately doubled (4)

annotation.definition: It holds large quantity of alcohol

indicatorNotes.ultimately: ultimately means in the end, so the last letter of BUT
indicatorNotes.doubled: made twice over, so that last letter appears again

annotation.surface: Talk of a distillery whose output is run through the still twice.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Still' sits among alcohol words as the distilling apparatus; it is the conjunction meaning nevertheless.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a butt is a large cask, traditionally holding wine or ale.

entries.clue: Go nuts, giving a twirl (4)

indicatorNotes.giving a twirl: a twirl spins something right round, so the word ends up backwards

annotation.surface: A dancer going wild with a spin.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Go nuts' reads as one phrase, to go crazy; split it, and 'Go' is the definition, as in 'have a go'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a go at something is an attempt, and so is a stab at it.

entries.clue: He leaves the lecture in an emotional state (7)

indicatorNotes.leaves: someone who leaves goes away, so HE departs from the letters

annotation.surface: A man walking out of a talk, overcome with feeling.
annotation.walkthrough: 'He' is not the man in the scene but the two letters, taken out of 'the'.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive paraphrase: tearful means close to crying, one particular emotional state.

entries.clue: Hack off lizard’s tail with inarticulate sound? Man perhaps admits it (10)

indicatorNotes.tail: a tail is the end of an animal, so the last letter of the word
indicatorNotes.admits: to admit is to let in, so ISLE lets GRUNT inside

annotation.surface: Chopping off a lizard's tail, and a man grunting about it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Man' is not a person but the Isle of Man, between Britain and Ireland. 'Hack off' is British slang for annoy.
annotation.definitionFit: A regional idiom: in British slang to hack someone off is to annoy them, to disgruntle them.

entries.clue: Someone who sells fish turned over a kipper? (7)

indicatorNotes.turned over: something turned over is flipped end to end, so the chain reads backwards

annotation.surface: A fishmonger flipping a smoked herring.
annotation.walkthrough: A kipper is a smoked herring, which fits the fishmonger; the definition means one who kips.
annotation.definitionFit: A pun on a regional word: to kip is British slang for to sleep, so a kipper is a sleeper.

entries.clue: 50 old songs played at gig coming up, including It’s Not Unusual? (7)

indicatorNotes.coming up: coming up means rising, which in a down clue means read from the bottom
indicatorNotes.including: to include something is to hold it within, so the letters take IT inside

blocks.note: a band's set, read upwards as TES

annotation.surface: A gig of old songs, including Tom Jones's hit It's Not Unusual.
annotation.walkthrough: The song title is split: 'It' is wordplay, the 's is a link, and 'Not Unusual' is an instance of the figure of speech, hence the question mark.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: litotes is understatement by denying the opposite, and 'not unusual' for common is a textbook case.

entries.clue: Sunny capital of Eritrea maybe pedestrianised around the outside (8)

indicatorNotes.capital of: a capital is an upper-case letter, and a word's capital is its first letter
indicatorNotes.around the outside: placed round the outside of something, so CARFREE encloses E

annotation.surface: A travel note: the Eritrean capital with its sunny, pedestrian-only streets.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Capital of Eritrea' sends you to Asmara; it is only the capital letter E.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for a temperament: a sunny, cheerful person is carefree.

entries.clue: As yet struggling to dress wife covered in beads (6)

indicatorNotes.struggling: something struggling thrashes about, so its letters fall out of order
indicatorNotes.to dress: to dress someone is to wrap clothes round them, so the letters wrap round W

annotation.surface: A husband still failing to get his bejewelled wife dressed.
annotation.walkthrough: The beads look like jewellery for the wife; they are beads of sweat.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic paraphrase: the beads are drops of perspiration, and skin covered in them is sweaty.

entries.clue: What’s up with album’s mindless followers? (5)

indicatorNotes.up: in a down clue, going up means the letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: an EP is a short record; the 's is 'has', joining it to the definition

annotation.surface: Asking what's happening with a band's brainless fans.
annotation.walkthrough: 'What's up' reads as a greeting, but it is the word 'what's' written upwards.
annotation.definitionFit: A figurative use: people who follow the crowd without thinking are called sheep.

entries.clue: Scottish runner offering to conserve energy now (3,3,7)

indicatorNotes.conserve: to conserve is to keep safe inside, so the pair holds E between them

blocks.note: the River Forth, which flows past Edinburgh
E = energy, held between the two
a present = a gift, an offering

annotation.surface: A Scottish athlete promising to save strength for later.
annotation.walkthrough: The 'runner' is a river, a crossword staple: the Forth is a Scottish river.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: for the present means for the time being, as things stand now.

entries.clue: Soldiers see gun (3)

annotation.surface: An order to troops to look at a weapon.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gun' is not the weapon but the verb, as in gunning an engine.
annotation.definitionFit: A verb sense: gunning an engine means pressing the accelerator hard, the same as revving it.

entries.clue: On vacation, Croatian houses dear in Split (6)

indicatorNotes.On vacation: a place on vacation is vacated, emptied of its middle
indicatorNotes.houses: a house holds people, so CN holds LOVE inside

blocks.note: love and dear are both terms of endearment

annotation.surface: Holiday lettings: Croatian homes for rent in Split.
annotation.walkthrough: Split is the Croatian port, which the surface sets up perfectly; the definition is the adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: cloven is the old past participle of cleave, so split, as in a cloven hoof.

entries.clue: Sort of music that is at a higher tempo than the rest (8)

annotation.definition: at a higher tempo than the rest
annotation.surface: A remark about a style of music played faster than all others.
annotation.walkthrough: The tempo talk keeps the music going, but the definition describes the answer, not the genre.
annotation.definitionFit: A superlative paraphrase: rapidest means fastest of all, going quicker than every other.
